title: Nontransitive dice
hook: Three dice where A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A, like rock, paper, scissors.
peek: Some dice break the usual rule that if A beats B and B beats C, then A must beat C. Whichever die your opponent picks, there is another that beats it more often than not. The trick is to let them choose first.
lede: We expect "better than" to work in a chain: if A beats B and B beats C, A should beat C. Certain dice break that rule. With the right numbers on their faces, each die in a set beats the next one more often than not, and the last beats the first. There is no best die, only a best reply.

bullets.text: Give die A the faces 2, 2, 4, 4, 9, 9; die B 1, 1, 6, 6, 8, 8; and die C 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7. Rolled against each other, A beats B, B beats C and C beats A, each with odds of 5 in 9.
The statistician Bradley Efron designed a set of four dice in which each beats the next with odds of 2 in 3. The puzzle writer Martin Gardner made them famous in a 1970 column.

The story goes that Warren Buffett once offered Bill Gates a game with nontransitive dice and invited him to pick first. Gates, suspicious, studied the dice and suggested Buffett choose first instead.
The mathematician James Grime designed a set with a second twist. Roll one of each die and the winning order goes one way. Roll two of each and add them up, and part of the order flips.
